Iran says US naval blockade is limiting petrol imports

Iran has been unable to import enough petrol to make up for a shortfall in domestic production because of a US naval blockade, a senior Iranian official said on Wednesday.

“Petrol production is insufficient, and because of the US naval blockade, we cannot import it,” Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah was quoted as saying by Iran’s state news agency IRNA.

His comments came as long queues formed outside petrol stations across Iran in recent days, with the US war effort increasingly shifting towards economic pressure on Tehran.

On Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s chief of staff, Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei, said the country’s petrol quotas would be reviewed, without providing further details.

The war began on 28 February, with Tehran subsequently taking control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

Ghaempanah also criticised Iran’s heavily subsidised fuel distribution system, saying it disproportionately benefits people who own multiple vehicles.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Badenoch must answer for the Tories' blanket support for Israel
item.description:
Badenoch must answer for the Tories' blanket support for Israel

Submitted by Peter Oborne on Wed, 08/26/2026 - 15:45
Despite ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people, the UK Conservative Party remains staunchly allied with the Netanyahu regime
UK Tory leader Kemi Badenoch speaks in London earlier this month (Justin Tallis/AFP)
Off

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s change of stance on Israel is popular in Britain, though many consider that it comes much too late and does not go far enough.

It has naturally been condemned by Israel, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu denouncing the “Islamic Republic of Britain” and Foreign Minister Gideon Saar slapping down his counterpart, Ed Miliband, for his “patronising tone”.

Israel can, however, continue to rely on one significant supporter: Kemi Badenoch’s Conservative Party.

According to the latest polling, 62 percent of British voters oppose Israel’s ongoing military actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, with a mere 13 percent in support. 

More than half want to end all arms sales to Israel, with only 22 percent in opposition. These figures are not surprising, since half of British voters have come to believe that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

When voter sentiment is as strong as this, it is most unusual for political parties to ignore it. Yet Badenoch offers near-blind support for Netanyahu. 

We can find no example of the Tory leader ever seriously criticising Israel over the annihilation of Gaza, the settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, or the bloody incursions into Lebanon. 

When the United States and Israel launched their catastrophic assault on Iran, Badenoch flung her weight behind the fiasco. Indeed, her admiration for Israel is so strong that she has condemned Reform UK leader Nigel Farage for being insufficiently supportive of Israel.

Sharp departure

Again and again, Badenoch echoes Netanyahu’s central claim that Israel is fighting a battle for western civilisation in Gaza. “Supporting Israel is not just right - it is necessary for our own national security,” the Tory leader wrote in the Sunday Times last year. “Israelis are at the front line in the fight for the West and for our shared values.”

This level of support marks a sharp departure from traditional Tory policy. Badenoch’s predecessor (and personal political heroine) Margaret Thatcher certainly stood up for Israel, but her backing was never unconditional. 

For example, Thatcher denounced the 1982 massacres in Lebanon committed by Christian Phalangists, with the Israeli army’s complicity, as “pure barbarism”. It is extremely difficult to imagine Badenoch using this kind of language to condemn contemporary Israeli atrocities.

Badenoch's adamant support for Israel does not just differentiate her from Thatcher and other Tory leaders. It also makes her Conservatives an outlier among European centre-right parties

In 1982, when Israel invaded Lebanon, Thatcher told Ronald Reagan, then the US president, that a “balanced policy” was best, and that “unlimited support for Israel can only lead to growing polarisation and despair in the Arab world”. Such measured statecraft appears beyond the capacity of Badenoch.

Thatcher, moreover, stood up for international law, while Badenoch mocks it. When the incoming Starmer government called time on former prime minister Rishi Sunak’s policy of undermining the International Criminal Court’s attempts to investigate Israeli (and Hamas) war crimes, Badenoch announced that Labour had “cowed to the mob”. 

On Israel and Palestine, Badenoch regularly twists the truth and ignores basic facts. She has accused Iran of orchestrating the 7 October 2023 attack, despite the assessment of the US director of national intelligence, published in February 2024, that “Iranian leaders did not orchestrate nor had foreknowledge of the Hamas attack against Israel”. 

Last year, she called Israel “a vibrant democracy that protects women and minorities and encourages them to vote, speak and dissent”.

These comments were made years after a consensus emerged among human rights groups - including Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Israel’s B’Tselem - that Israel practises apartheid.

An apartheid state cannot be democratic. Badenoch ignored the opinion of international authorities to say that Israel was a democracy, when in fact it rules over millions of Palestinians with no rights.

Vested interest 

Badenoch’s position on Israel was arguably constrained by her role as business and trade secretary in Sunak’s government. This meant it fell to her to approve arms sales to Israel, which she continued to do during a period when Israel was accused of genocide.

If the International Court of Justice (ICJ) determines that Israel has indeed committed genocide, the judgment will open Badenoch herself up to charges that she was an accomplice, alongside senior Tory colleagues. She thus cannot accuse Israel of criminality (at least in the period until July 2024) without risking incriminating herself.

In common with all senior Tories from the last government, Badenoch therefore has a vested interest in denying Israeli atrocities.

Badenoch’s adamant support for Israel does not just differentiate her from Thatcher and other Tory leaders. It also makes her Conservatives an outlier among European centre-right parties. 

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni suspended defence cooperation with Israel earlier this year. In Germany, the strongly pro-Israel Merz government in August 2025 announced a halt to exports of arms to Israel that could be used in Gaza. 

Although Germany lifted this partial suspension of arms exports after the “ceasefire” was called, it is striking that Badenoch has never supported such a suspension.

In May 2025, France and Canada joined Britain in condemning Israel’s “egregious actions” in Gaza, in response to renewed military operations, obstruction of aid, and threats to permanently displace the Palestinian population. 

Shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel attacked this statement by saying that Hamas had supported the French, Canadian and British position.        

The Tories’ position seems closest to that of France’s extreme-right National Rally, whose president, Jordan Bardella, said during a recent visit to Israel that its “war in the face of barbarism … is also our fight”. 

Questions unanswered

This week, Middle East Eye wrote to the Conservative Party with a series of questions. We asked for evidence that Iran orchestrated the 7 October attacks.

We asked whether Badenoch’s approval of arms sales to Israel during her time as business and trade secretary had compromised her ability to impartially judge whether Israel’s actions are criminal.  

We asked whether Badenoch accepted the July 2024 opinion of the ICJ - and human rights organisations including B’Tselem, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International - that Israel has breached the legal prohibition of apartheid. 

We asked whether any member of the leadership of the Conservative Party has criticised the large-scale torture of Palestinian detainees by Israel (our own searches have not revealed any such criticism).

Badenoch blurts out the truth: Britain is at the heart of Gaza 'proxy war'
Read More »

We asked whether Badenoch believes that Israel has committed any war crimes in Gaza since October 2023.

We pointed out that Badenoch’s foreign affairs spokesperson, Patel, resigned from her office as international development secretary after holding unauthorised meetings with Israeli officials in 2017, and we asked: “In view of Patel’s failure to uphold transparency and openness in dealing with foreign officials, why did Kemi Badenoch appoint Priti Patel shadow foreign secretary?”

We sent these questions several times to the Conservative Party, giving ample time to reply, but received no answer.

These questions matter very much. Miliband is expected to soon announce a series of punitive measures against Israel in response to settler violence and settlement expansion - a programme that, in the light of the E1 development, threatens to destroy any possibility of an independent Palestinian state.

So we wrote: “Kemi Badenoch has strongly opposed Labour’s recognition of a Palestinian State. The Conservative Party, however, claims to support a two-state solution. How can the Conservative Party support a two-state solution while granting recognition to Israel, and refusing to recognise Palestine?”

We sent this question more than once to the Conservative Party. We received no answer.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Iranian press review: Principlists warn that regional mediation could be US trap
item.description:
Iranian press review: Principlists warn that regional mediation could be US trap

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Thu, 08/27/2026 - 10:00
Meanwhile, there's a mixed response to new US sanctions, former diplomat criticises 'too much courtesy' towards Gulf states, and Sharif university expels six dissident students
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (R) meets with Oman's Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi in Tehran, 25 August 2026 (Iranian foreign ministry/Wana/Handout via Reuters)
Off

Principlists warn of 'US deception' in talks

Recent efforts by Pakistan and Oman to mediate between Iran and the US have been met with scepticism from Iran’s principlist camp, which views regional diplomatic initiatives as part of Washington’s efforts to mislead Tehran and alter its calculations.

The Kayhan daily, an outlet close to this camp, described the visits by Pakistani and Omani officials to Tehran as part of a “new phase in the White House’s deception operation”.

This scepticism towards mediation stems from the fact that the US and Israel have, on two occasions so far, launched attacks while negotiations with Iran were under way; an experience that has contributed to deeper distrust of any proposal for negotiations or a ceasefire.

The daily wrote that Washington, after its failure on the battlefield with Iran, and amid increased economic pressure, is using regional mediators to find a way out of the current situation.

Kayhan went on to emphasise the need to maintain military pressure and deliver a tough response to the US. It wrote: “In the face of every suspension of US withdrawal from agreements (such as what happened in previous agreements), Washington will face broader demands and stronger conditions [from Tehran], including the complete lifting of the blockade, the release of all frozen funds, the lifting of sanctions, and the practical withdrawal of military forces.”

Farsi outlets react to latest US sanctions

Most Iranian newspapers led their front pages on Tuesday with headlines about the potential impact of new US sanctions. The coverage came a day after Washington announced the measures.

Outlets close to reformists addressed Iran's economic conditions and the need to solve these problems. Meanwhile, newspapers close to conservative and hardline groups focused on the "ineffectiveness" of the sanctions and Iran's ability to bypass them.

Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ tests Iran’s trading ties across the region
Read More »

The pro-reformist Etemad daily reviewed the problems facing President Masoud Pezeshkian’s government, highlighting the budget deficit, a lack of investment, the US naval blockade and decades of economic sanctions as the main obstacles to improving people's livelihoods.

On the other side of the political spectrum, the Kayhan daily called the new sanctions a political bluff, writing that the US announced the measures without having the necessary tools.

The Javan daily, funded by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, echoed Kayhan's viewpoint. It covered the intensification of the US economic war under the headline: "Trump Plants 'D-Day', Reaps 'Waterloo'".

In its report, Javan wrote: "This is a boomerang that returns to America, affecting everything from inflation and interest rates to government financing costs and the treasury bond market. Tightening the rope does not only choke Iran's throat; in a long war, it also narrows America's airways."

Diplomat urges tougher policy towards Gulf

With no end in sight to the military confrontation between Washington and Tehran, the situation has rekindled debate over how Iran should deal with Arab states in the region.

Mohammad Masjed-Jamei, a former Iranian ambassador, has called for a firmer approach toward the Gulf "sheikhdoms" and criticised what he sees as excessive politeness in Iran’s policy towards them.

Iran's new Security Council shake-up reveals growing divisions over US deal
Read More »

Speaking about the Arab states on the southern side of the Gulf, Masjed-Jamei described Saudi Arabia not as the “older brother” but as the “dominant power” in the region. He said Saudi Arabia’s foreign policy “acts as a cause of tension”. He also said that the United Arab Emirates “plays a role far beyond its real capacity”.

Masjed-Jamei suggested that one of Iran’s main problems in dealing with the Gulf states was an approach that was “too much based on courtesy, polite talk, and emphasis on brotherhood and friendship”. He added: “You should not try too hard to get a smile from the other side.” 

Masjed-Jamei also cited Turkey as an example of a country that works with the Gulf states while taking a firm position towards them. He argued that Iran should also deal with the Arab states in the region according to its “weight, size, position and history”.

Pressure increases on university students 

As the new academic year approaches in Iran, disciplinary proceedings continue against students at Sharif University of Technology, with expulsion orders issued against six students, local media reported.

Mahmoud Bahmanabadi, Sharif University’s deputy for student affairs, said that 236 students were referred to the disciplinary committee in connection with anti-establishment protests in January. 

The university opened disciplinary cases against 115 of them after finding sufficient evidence, according to the university. Around 40 students accused of more serious violations were also summoned before the disciplinary committee.

Bahmanabadi said that “so far, six people who attempted to burn the sacred flag of the Islamic Republic or raised the flag of the monarchists at the university have received expulsion orders”. 

The university also said that other disciplinary decisions included written reprimands and suspension from studies for one or two semesters.

Two girls walk amid the rubble in Khan Younis in southern Gaza, on 25 August (AFP/Bashar Taleb)

The head of a coalition of aid groups has warned that the US-backed Board of Peace is "failing" in Gaza and has “functioned to further entrench Israel’s unlawful presence" in the territory.

Athena Rayburn, executive director of the Association of International Development Agencies (AIDA), told the UN Security Council that the organisation – established by US President Donald Trump and given a mandate by the council in November – was enabling Israel's obstruction of humanitarian aid.

She said Israel was rejecting scissors, crutches, wheelchairs and prosthetic limbs as “dual-use” instruments, has barred specialised medical staff, and placed restrictions on engine oil so severe that it cost 45 times its normal price.

Israel also rejected watermelon and onions under an unpublished “humanitarian policy”.

"What is unclear is why the mandate handed by this council to the Board of Peace is being used to violate the most fundamental rights of the Palestinians in Gaza and the most basic rules of humanitarian law," Rayburn said. "This cannot be the new status quo."

At least 1,303 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since a supposed ceasefire began in October 2025.

So far, a total of 73,438 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the genocide in October 2023.

'Point of no return'

Israel now controls more than 60 percent of the enclave, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu even saying earlier this month that the aim is to increase to around 70 percent.

The Board of Peace has linked any Israeli withdrawal beyond the Yellow Line – which divides Gaza into areas occupied by Israeli and Palestinian control – to the complete disarmament of Hamas.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Meta agrees to make sweeping changes to apps for teens | First Thing
item.description:
Safety features including usage limits and night-time blocks to be set by default. Plus changes to famous French cheeses

  • Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. Meta has agreed to significant changes to its Instagram and Facebook apps in a settlement that ended a landmark lawsuit. The agreement curtails a major trial in California and will require the social media company to pay up to $18bn. Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use nationwide in the US.

California and 28 other US states sued the $1.36tn (£1tn) company over allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. As part of the settlement, the company denies wrongdoing.

What will be changing in the apps? The biggest alteration is that Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, is now required to make many of its safety limitations the default setting for accounts created by teenagers, a pivot from its previous opt-in approach to child safety. Nick Robins-Early and Johana Bhuiyan explain more in this piece: six key takeaways from the end of the Meta trial.

Will other companies be affected? Meta is putting the agreement forward as a precedent for other social media companies to follow. The company’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said: “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers … to implement this new framework.” Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap face thousands more similar US lawsuits brought by families, individuals, school districts and other attorneys general.

Are campaigners satisfied with the result? Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the outcome “is not an all-clear to say the product is safe. The limitations that are in the agreement are the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day’. It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

Criminal gangs have expelled Palestinians and looted homes while serving as an 'operational arm' of Israel’s military
Palestinians inspect the damage at the site of an Israeli air strike in Gaza City on 24 August (AFP/Omar Al Qattaa)

The Israeli army is expanding its use of mercenaries, criminal gangs and drug dealers to commit “war crimes” on Israel’s behalf in Gaza, an investigation by the Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz has revealed.

Based on testimony from Israeli soldiers, UN reports and satellite imagery, the investigation found that increasingly well-armed collaborator militias have expelled Palestinians from their homes and carried out operations across Gaza.

Israel has trained at least five militia groups, and potentially a sixth, operating from heavily fortified bases inside Israeli-occupied areas of the enclave.

One Israeli soldier described how the state, army and Shin Bet intelligence service send armed and “trained militias to commit war crimes, and I'm the one who has to protect them during their operations so they don't get hurt”.

The Israeli army has itself committed war crimes across Gaza.

Israel faces a genocide case at the International Court of Justice, while the International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity.

At least one militia armed and supported by Israel had links to the Islamic State group. Its leader, Yasser Abu Shabab, was killed by Hamas in December 2025.

Many Palestinians celebrated Abu Shabab’s death, while his own family had renounced him as a traitor for collaborating with Israel.

“But the militia project he came to symbolize continues to evolve and expand – particularly since the October 2025 ceasefire was announced,” Haaretz reported.

'They entered every structure, looted everything they could get their hands on, came out with piles of stuff – and then burned down the house'

– Unnamed Israeli soldier

Another militia leader, Shawqi Abu Nasira, openly acknowledged his collaboration with Israel in a video posted online.

“I made the decision to liberate the land from Hamas. If people say that makes me a collaborator, then I'm a collaborator.”

The vast majority of Palestinians view collaboration with Israel as treason and betrayal, regardless of their position on Hamas.

Israel has also built infrastructure for the gangs amid Gaza’s widespread destruction. Near a militia base in Shujaiya, Israeli forces levelled a large Palestinian cemetery and replaced it with an extensive training ground.

The relationship between the gangs and the Israeli military has become increasingly intertwined. Fighters roam freely around Israeli army outposts, according to soldiers who spoke to Haaretz.

“The gunmen stage displays of force, film them and upload the footage to their Facebook pages for propaganda and recruitment purposes,” the investigation said.

Israel supplies the gangs with weapons and provides artillery and drone support during their operations.

'Reminiscent of Sabra and Shatila '

The mercenaries also serve another purpose. They attack Palestinians struggling to survive Israel’s genocide, drive families from their homes, loot their belongings and burn their houses.

Israeli ministers have repeatedly called for making life in Gaza unbearable as part of efforts to ethnically cleanse the enclave and replace its Palestinian population with Jewish settlers.

In one account, Israeli soldiers said the mercenaries arrived in pickup trucks before “they just ran and shot at people”.

“They entered every structure, looted everything they could get their hands on, came out with piles of stuff – and then burned down the house," one unnamed Israeli soldier said.

Reports that Israel has used local gangs to outsource parts of its strategy to ethnically cleanse Gaza are not new. Their activities have been documented for more than a year.

The soldiers’ testimony, however, provides further evidence that the mercenaries now function as an “operational arm” of the Israeli army and Shin Bet.

Israel continues to arm criminal gangs while demanding that Hamas disarm and opposing the formation of any independent Palestinian security force in Gaza. The arrangement allows Israel to use the militias against anyone it labels a Hamas member while unleashing them against ordinary Palestinians.

Hamas sources told Haaretz that they would not surrender their “defensive weapons” while the militias remain armed and receive Israeli support, because the groups would seek to target them.

Haaretz said “alarm bells are ringing” that Israel may be creating the conditions for local “atrocities reminiscent of the Sabra and Shatila massacre”.

During the 1982 massacre, Israeli-allied Lebanese Phalangist forces slaughtered up to 3,500 Palestinian and Lebanese civilians as Israeli troops surrounded the Beirut refugee camps and oversaw the killing.

Israeli authorities have replaced “Damascus Gate” with “Ancient Gate” on public signs in occupied East Jerusalem, in what critics describe as a further attempt to erase the city’s Palestinian identity.

Damascus Gate, on the northern side of Jerusalem’s Old City, is one of the most prominent entrances through its ancient walls.

It is also a main route for Palestinians travelling to Al-Aqsa Mosque and a key social gathering point.

Earlier this week, signs bearing the name Damascus Gate were removed and replaced with “Ancient Gate” in Arabic, English and Hebrew.

Abdullah Marouf, a researcher specialising in Al-Aqsa Mosque affairs, said Israel was seeking to Judaise Jerusalem by replacing Arabic and Islamic symbols in public life with Jewish ones.

He said the area around Damascus Gate was a vital part of daily life for Palestinians and that Israel had long sought to change its name.

“This Hebrew name aims to strip the place of its ‘Damascus Gate’ designation, as it is one of the main and central gates of Jerusalem,” Marouf told Middle East Eye.

Attempts to rename landmarks in the area are not new, Marouf said.

Israel previously renamed Solomon’s Cave, between Damascus Gate and Herod’s Gate, as “Zedekiah’s Cave”.

Such names, Marouf said, were intended to alter the character and identity of Jerusalem.

“Israel has proven its utter failure in achieving this goal, as the image, nature and Arabic language of Jerusalem are clear, and a sign in one of the city’s streets cannot change its reality,” he said.

The latest change comes amid a wider campaign targeting street names, landmarks and historical sites across Jerusalem.

The Jerusalem Governorate said Israeli authorities were replacing long-standing Arabic names as part of a policy to reshape the city’s urban and cultural landscape.

In a statement on Wednesday, the governorate said the changes were not simply administrative measures but part of a broader effort to sever future generations from the city’s historical Arabic names.

“The names of Jerusalem’s gates, streets and landmarks represent an integral part of the city’s national, historical and cultural memory,” it said.

“Replacing them with new names undermines Jerusalem’s identity and its Arab, Islamic and Christian heritage.”

The governorate warned that such measures would not erase Jerusalem’s history or its national and cultural memory.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Why Turkey is showing restraint over Israeli strikes on Syria
item.description:
Why Turkey is showing restraint over Israeli strikes on Syria

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Thu, 08/27/2026 - 12:10
Ankara is counting on possible political change in Israel while using its relationship with Washington to advance its objectives in Syria
Turkish cavalry guards waving the Israeli (R) and Turkish flags to welcome the Israeli president to Ankara on 9 March 2022 (Handout Israeli Government Press Office/AFP)
Off

Turkey is likely to maintain its restraint in responding to Israeli attacks on Syria until after Israel’s general election in October, as Ankara does not want to throw a lifeline to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s struggling election campaign.

Although Israeli strikes on the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in northern Syria, approximately 70km from the Turkish border, were seen as provocative, they did not surprise officials in Ankara.

Israel claimed that Turkey was preparing to deploy air defence systems at the base.

“Israel has hit other bases in Syria before. There is nothing particularly important about this one,” one Turkish official told Middle East Eye.

The official added that the Turkish government had clearly conveyed its position on Israel’s actions through multiple public statements. Ankara believes Netanyahu is under intense pressure at home and is seeking a way out by escalating tensions with Turkey.

“And he is a madman, definitely, for trying that,” the official added.

Many Ankara insiders expect the Israeli election to result in a change of government and bring more reasonable politicians to power. Turkish officials point to opposition from some Israeli politicians to the escalation triggered by Netanyahu, including Yair Golan, a former general and chairman of the left-wing Democrats party.

Israel’s decision not to use the hotline between the two governments during the strikes on the Syrian airbase is seen as particularly dangerous.

Another provocative factor is Israel’s apparent violation of understandings reached with Ankara during talks in Baku last year.

Violation of previous understanding

A regional official familiar with consultations between Turkish and Israeli officials told MEE that both sides had agreed that the area north of the T4 airbase, near Palmyra, would form a dividing line in Syria between Israeli and Turkish security zones.

T4 had been a particular point of contention for the Israeli government, because Ankara wanted to turn it into a drone base for operations against the Islamic State, which has a strong presence around Palmyra.

Israel bombed the base before the Turkish military could move in, prompting the two sides to begin talks on a deconfliction mechanism.

The agreement on a dividing line stemmed from Israel’s request to maintain an air corridor through Syria for potential strikes on Iran in the event of a war.

The regional official added that Israel continued to oppose the deployment of Turkish radars and air defence systems in Syria but had been relatively satisfied with the progress made in talks.

However, last week’s strikes indicate that Israel now wants to forcibly impose its opposition to any Turkish-supported or Turkish-armed airbase in northern Syria, including in areas very close to the Turkish border.

Ankara says it has made no attempt to deploy forces to the Abu al-Duhur airbase – a position supported by statements from Syrian and US officials. Turkey therefore views the Israeli strikes as a violation of the previous understanding.

Israeli government complains about status-quo broken, but latest attack changes the "status quo" that Israel had already, in some form agreed to, as shown on the map. Israel is naturally unhappy because, for many years, it had complete freedom to fly over Syrian territory and… pic.twitter.com/xLnv6f4RVr

— Dünya Başol (@dunya_basol) August 19, 2026

Several Turkish officials told MEE that Ankara no longer considers the current Israeli government a rational actor.

The officials said Ankara had demonstrated to the world that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, rather than Netanyahu, was acting rationally and with restraint in addressing regional issues.

Despite the strikes and repeated insulting statements from Netanyahu, Erdogan did not cut short his holiday to make an announcement. Instead, he was filmed last Friday joking with local politicians near Marmaris, where he often spends his summer holidays.

When Erdogan emerged on Tuesday, he again avoided directly mentioning Israel or Netanyahu. He said he would not dignify “murderous networks” seeking political gains for their failing election campaigns by addressing them directly.

However, he forcefully reiterated that Ankara had a plan for the region and would not abandon its friends. He also said Turkey had no secret objectives and sought only to promote peace.

Turkey playing 'long game in Syria'

One reason Turkey has responded calmly and cautiously in Syria is that Netanyahu’s relationship with US President Donald Trump has deteriorated significantly over the past year.

Netanyahu’s maximalist demands regarding Iran, Lebanon and Gaza have often put Trump at odds with regional realities and key Arab allies.

Turkey recruits Trump insiders for new Washington lobbying push
Read More »

Rather than confronting Netanyahu directly, Turkey has followed Washington’s lead. In this case, the Turkish leadership’s decision to establish close ties with US special envoy Thomas Barrack played an important role in strengthening Ankara’s position.

Thanks to the strong rapport between Trump and Erdogan, Ankara this week overcame a series of Israeli objections concerning Syria.

First, the US State Department has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, after 47 years. The move came as Israeli officials continued to describe Syria’s interim president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, as an extremist and a “militia leader”.

The department also revoked the designation of Sharaa’s former group, the al-Nusra Front – also known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) – as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organisation.

Second, despite Israeli efforts to preserve a Syria with a weak central government or divided into separate entities, Mazloum Abdi, the commander-in-chief of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, announced the full integration of his forces into the Damascus government and the abolition of the self-declared autonomous zone. This represented another victory for Turkey.

“Turkey is playing a long game in Syria,” a second Turkish official said. “Unlike the Israelis, we prioritise a stable, sovereign and prosperous country that would strengthen security and peace across the region.”

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How will Iran respond to Trump's 'economic D-Day'?
item.description:
How will Iran respond to Trump's 'economic D-Day'?

Submitted by Shahir Shahidsaless on Wed, 08/26/2026 - 20:10
By steadily narrowing Tehran's options, Washington could eventually make escalation appear less a choice than a necessity
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian attends a news conference in the capital Tehran, on 8 August 2026 (Iranian Presidential Office/AFP)
Off

After days of intense buildup, the Trump administration has unveiled what it calls “economic D-Day” against Iran. 

US Treasury Secretary Bessent vowed the toughest sanctions campaign in history, following President Donald Trump’s threat to “crush” Iran with economic warfare “on an unprecedented scale” unless Tehran surrendered to Washington’s demands.

Yet the sanctions regime Bessent described on Monday came with surprisingly few specifics. Even before the announcement, thousands of Iranian and non-Iranian individuals and entities were already facing US sanctions. 

The apparent novelty lies less in sanctioning Iran itself than in threatening countries, companies and financial networks that continue doing business with Tehran. Bessent even borrowed a page from former US president George W Bush’s playbook: “You are either with us or against us.”

According to Iranian customs data, the country trades with 178 states, but China and the UAE matter most. 

China is Iran’s biggest buyer of oil. The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission says Beijing purchases “upward of 90 percent” of Iranian crude exports. 

The UAE, meanwhile, has long been a crucial conduit connecting Iran to global commerce, and helping it circumvent sanctions. According to data from the World Trade Organization, in 2024, Iran obtained 30.6 percent of its imports, worth roughly $21bn, from the UAE. 

That figure alone does not capture the wider role of front companies, banking channels and Dubai-based exchange houses in facilitating Iranian trade.

Bigger test

The UAE has now announced a halt to Iran-related trade and transactions, a move Bessent said “was not a coincidence”. But how much bilateral commerce was still functioning is unclear. 

Since the war began, the UAE has suffered more Iranian missile and drone attacks than any other regional state, with nearly 3,000 directed at it. The announcement might therefore merely formalise a rupture the war had already largely brought about.

China is the bigger test. Asked whether Beijing would be targeted, Bessent replied that “no one is above the reach of US sanctions”. 

China immediately pushed back, with foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian warning that the measures would intensify tensions, and vowing that Beijing would take “all necessary measures” to protect its interests.

Is this a genuinely new sanctions architecture backed by much harsher enforcement, or partly psychological warfare, intended to convince Tehran that economic collapse is inevitable unless it capitulates?

Washington has tested this before. In May, after the US sanctioned five Chinese refineries buying Iranian oil, Beijing reportedly instructed them to ignore the sanctions and offered protection. That raises the central question: is Washington really prepared for a wider economic confrontation with China over Iran?

There is a broader problem. A campaign of this scale requires extensive international cooperation, yet Trump has simultaneously opened trade and political conflicts with allies and rivals alike, from Canada and Europe to China. The international environment is far removed from the Obama years, when even China and Russia supported UN Security Council sanctions against Iran.

Meanwhile, sanctions are operating alongside a maritime blockade that has already caused a steep fall in Iranian oil exports. So what exactly is Bessent adding? Is this a genuinely new sanctions architecture backed by much harsher enforcement, or partly psychological warfare, intended to convince Tehran that economic collapse is inevitable unless it capitulates?

There might also be a market-psychology dimension. The Trump administration has every incentive to blunt the domestic economic consequences of the war. This August, the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline is shaping up to be the highest on record. Trump and his administration have repeatedly claimed that oil is pouring through Hormuz, but vessel trackers can’t find it. 

Whatever the longer-term effects, Bessent’s announcement worked immediately: stocks rose, Brent fell sharply, and the bond market calmed.

Plausible trajectories

The pivotal question is how Tehran responds. From Iran’s perspective, the present situation cannot continue indefinitely.

The debate over what to do next is already visible inside the leadership. President Masoud Pezeshkian and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who heads Iran’s negotiating team, have emphasised both the economic dangers of prolonging the conflict and the need for a settlement. 

On 21 August, Ghalibaf made an unusually blunt admission: “No matter how much military power we have, if people are hungry, we will not endure.” Pezeshkian argued the same day that Iran should end the war now, while it still considers itself in a position of strength.

On the other side, Mohsen Rezaei, recently appointed secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Iran’s highest security body, appears to favour greater counter-pressure. Rezaei and the supreme leader have opposed the Pezeshkian-Ghalibaf approach since the Islamabad negotiations. 

Against this backdrop, three trajectories appear plausible, in what I see as descending order of likelihood.

First, Tehran may try to hold out until the 3 November US congressional elections, calculating that a Democratic sweep of both chambers could give Congress the political and financial leverage to force Trump to wind down or end the war.

That possibility cannot be dismissed. Race to the White House, a data-driven election forecasting model that incorporates polling, electoral history, fundraising and other factors, and runs thousands of simulations after each update, currently gives Democrats a 76 percent chance of winning the House and a 53 percent chance of taking the Senate. 

More striking is the trend: just before the war, Republicans led Democrats 77 percent to 23 percent in the Senate forecast. Now Democrats lead 53 percent to 47 percent, a 60-point swing.

Until November, Tehran may therefore avoid major escalation, keep Hormuz effectively closed, and continue periodic attacks on tankers to maintain pressure on oil markets and, by extension, the Trump administration.

Renewed mediation

Second, a negotiated settlement could emerge before the elections through mediation channels that are becoming active again, particularly Pakistan and Oman. Iran would probably have to genuinely reopen Hormuz, abandon its demand that a settlement also end the Lebanon war, ensure that Houthi attacks cease, and reaffirm that it will not build a nuclear weapon.

Pakistan’s renewed mediation gives this scenario some substance. Shortly after Bessent’s announcement, hopes of negotiations helped push Brent below $88. 

Mohsin Naqvi, Pakistan’s interior minister, said on Monday that he and army chief Asim Munir had a “very positive and productive meeting” with the Iranian president, during which “significant progress was made”.

Naqvi added: “We remain hopeful that this momentum will help pave the way for further progress and lasting peace in the region.”

Third, Tehran could conclude that waiting has become more dangerous than escalation, and initiate another round of fighting.

Rezaei’s remarks last weekend provide a striking indication of what such a strategy could entail. He warned that although Iran had so far targeted only military bases, if Washington intensified its economic war, American oil and other commercial companies operating in the region could also become targets.

This was one of Tehran’s clearest recent threats to explicitly identify US oil companies as potential targets. American corporate activity and investment across the region, particularly in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, have expanded substantially in recent years.

The objective of renewed escalation would not necessarily be military victory. Rather, Tehran could seek to create a sufficiently severe shock to regional energy flows to drive oil prices sharply higher, raise US gasoline prices and inflation, and force Washington to reconsider the economic and political costs of continuing the war.

Bessent’s offensive may therefore have an unintended consequence. By steadily narrowing Tehran’s options, it could eventually make escalation appear less a choice than a necessity.
